title: WHY DID PHARAOH’S DAUGHTER SAVE THE BABY HER FATHER ORDERED TO BE KILLED?
paragraphs: WHY DID PHARAOH’S DAUGHTER SAVE THE BABY HER FATHER ORDERED TO BE KILLED?
She Was Raised in the House That Ordered His Death. But One Cry from a Hebrew Baby Changed Everything—and Exposed a Truth About God’s Mercy That Still Confronts Us Today.
“And when she had opened it, she saw the child: and, behold, the babe wept. And she had compassion on him, and said, This is one of the Hebrews’ children.” — Exodus 2:6 (KJV)
Imagine being born into a world where your first breath makes you a criminal.
You have committed no sin against the government. You have threatened no throne. You have spoken no rebellious word.
You are guilty of only one thing.
You were born into the wrong family, among the wrong people, under the rule of a man who has decided that children like you should not live.
And somewhere inside a palace, a young woman is about to discover that obedience to her father could mean becoming an accomplice to murder.
She has everything a person could desire.
Royal privilege. Protection. Servants. Influence. A future secured by the most powerful household in Egypt.
But the moment she opens a small basket floating among the reeds of the Nile, everything changes.
Inside is a crying baby.
She knows exactly who he is.
She knows what her father has commanded.
She knows that saving him means acting against the murderous policy of her own household.
And still...
She reaches for him.
What made her do it?

Was it maternal instinct? Compassion? A sudden realization that her father's command was evil? Was God working through a woman who did not yet understand the extraordinary role she would play in Israel's deliverance?
Scripture does not tell us everything happening inside her heart.
But it tells us enough to reveal something astonishing.
The daughter of the man who ordered Hebrew sons to die became the woman through whom one Hebrew son was preserved.
And that child would grow up to confront the very throne that had threatened his life.
His name was Moses.
But before we celebrate the miracle, we need to understand the horror that made it necessary.
Because the story did not begin with a princess discovering a baby.
It began with a nation trembling under the weight of fear.

Egypt had become a place of suffering for the descendants of Israel. What began generations earlier with Joseph's family finding refuge in Egypt had turned into bitter slavery under a new king who did not know Joseph.
The Israelites multiplied, and Pharaoh became afraid.
Their growing numbers were no longer seen as evidence of a thriving community. To Pharaoh, they represented a potential threat to his control.
Fear became suspicion.
Suspicion became oppression.
Oppression became state-sanctioned killing.
First, Pharaoh commanded the Hebrew midwives to kill the newborn boys while allowing the girls to live.
But two women, Shiphrah and Puah, feared God more than they feared the king.
Exodus 1:17 declares:
“But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men children alive.”
Their courage matters.
Before Pharaoh's daughter ever stepped into the story, God had already shown us women who refused to cooperate with evil.
Then Pharaoh escalated his command.
Exodus 1:22 records the chilling decree:
“Every son that is born ye shall cast into the river, and every daughter ye shall save alive.”
Think about what those words meant.
A mother holding her newborn son could no longer simply rejoice.
A father hearing his baby cry could no longer assume that the sound meant safety.
The river that sustained Egyptian civilization had been designated as an instrument of death for Hebrew boys.
And perhaps the most terrifying thing about Pharaoh's command was how easily an entire society could begin treating cruelty as obedience.
When evil receives the approval of powerful people, ordinary people face a choice.
Will they obey?
Will they look away?
Or will they recognize that no earthly authority possesses the right to overturn God's moral commands?
This is where the story becomes uncomfortably personal.
Because not every wicked command arrives with a royal seal.
Sometimes it arrives through family pressure.
Sometimes it comes from a workplace where dishonesty is expected.
Sometimes it comes from a culture that tells you to remain silent while vulnerable people are mistreated.
Sometimes the hardest thing you will ever do is refuse to become the kind of person your surroundings are encouraging you to be.
And that is why Pharaoh's daughter deserves our attention.
She lived inside the very household from which the decree came.
Yet the Bible introduces her not as an extension of her father's cruelty, but as a woman whose compassion would help preserve a life.
Meanwhile, somewhere beyond the palace walls, a Hebrew mother was facing an impossible decision.
Exodus 2 tells us that a woman from the tribe of Levi gave birth to a son.
She saw that he was a beautiful child and hid him for three months.
Imagine those months.
Every unexpected knock.
Every approaching footstep.
Every moment the baby cried too loudly.
Every night she wondered whether the next morning would bring soldiers to her door.
She loved her son.
But love could not make the danger disappear.
Eventually, she could hide him no longer.
So she prepared a small basket, coated it with materials that would help keep water out, placed her child inside, and laid it among the reeds beside the Nile.
The Hebrew word used for that basket is תֵּבָה (tevah).
It is a remarkable word.
In the Hebrew Bible, tevah is also the word used for Noah's ark in Genesis.
These are the two biblical narratives in which this particular Hebrew noun appears.
In Genesis, God preserves Noah and his family through the waters of judgment inside an ark.
In Exodus, a Hebrew mother places her endangered child inside a small ark-like vessel upon the waters of the Nile.
The word does not mean that the two events are identical. Nor does it prove that Moses' mother understood every part of God's future plan.
But the literary connection is powerful.
In both accounts, a vessel becomes a means of preserving life amid deadly waters.
The river Pharaoh intended to become a grave would become the setting of Moses' rescue.
And here is a detail we cannot afford to miss.
Moses' mother did not simply throw her child into the current and walk away.
She placed the basket among the reeds by the riverbank.
His sister stood at a distance, watching to see what would happen.
There was preparation.
There was courage.
There was unbearable uncertainty.
And there was a family doing everything within its power to preserve a life.
Perhaps you know something about that kind of moment.
Not because you have ever placed a child in a basket beside a river.
But because you have reached the limit of what your hands could hold.
You have prayed over a child whose future frightened you.
You have watched someone you love walk into circumstances you could not control.
You have done everything you knew to do, and still found yourself staring at a situation too large for your strength.
There are moments when faith does not look like confidence.
Sometimes faith looks like trembling hands doing the next faithful thing.
And then comes the moment that changes the story.
Exodus 2:5 says:
“And the daughter of Pharaoh came down to wash herself at the river; and her maidens walked along by the river's side; and when she saw the ark among the flags, she sent her maid to fetch it.”
The princess sees the basket.
She sends someone to retrieve it.
She opens it.
And inside...
A baby is crying.
The next verse contains the emotional center of the entire account.
“And she had compassion on him.”
In Hebrew, the phrase is:
וַתַּחְמֹל עָלָיו
Vattachmol alav.
A faithful rendering is:
“And she had compassion on him,” or “And she took pity on him.”
The verb comes from the Hebrew root חמל (ḥ-m-l), expressing pity, compassion, or sparing someone.
It is not merely a description of the princess noticing the child.
It describes her response to his vulnerability.
And the next words prove that she understood the danger.
“This is one of the Hebrews' children.”
She recognized that this was no ordinary abandoned baby.
He belonged to the very people her father had targeted.
She could have ordered the basket returned to the river.
She could have looked away.
She could have treated the infant as someone else's problem.
She could have allowed her father's decree to determine her response.
But she did not.
The text does not say that she delivered a speech against Pharaoh, publicly renounced Egyptian religion, or formally embraced Israel's God.
We must not add those claims to Scripture.
What Scripture actually records is already extraordinary.
She recognized a condemned Hebrew child, felt compassion, and chose to preserve his life.
That is the answer to the question.
Why did Pharaoh's daughter defy her father's order?
The explicit reason the narrative gives us is compassion.
The wider story also shows God's providence at work in preserving the future deliverer of Israel.
But Scripture does not reveal whether she fully understood the divine purpose behind her decision.
And perhaps that makes the account even more remarkable.
Because she did not need to know the child's future significance to recognize his present humanity.
She did not need to know he would become Moses.
She did not need to know he would stand before Pharaoh.
She did not need to know about the burning bush, the plagues, the Passover, or the parting of the Red Sea.
All she knew was that a vulnerable child needed mercy.
And she responded.
How many people have we overlooked because we could not see what God might do through their lives?
How many hurting people have we dismissed because their pain was inconvenient?
How many times have we waited for someone to prove they deserved kindness before we were willing to show it?
Pharaoh's daughter did not know the entire story.
She simply refused to let the baby die.
And that one act of compassion became part of a much greater story of deliverance.
But the surprises were not finished.
Moses' sister, who had been watching from a distance, approached the princess.
Exodus 2:7 records her question:
“Shall I go and call to thee a nurse of the Hebrew women, that she may nurse the child for thee?”
The princess agreed.
And the girl went to call the baby's own mother.
Read that again.
The mother who had been forced to surrender her son to save his life was brought back to care for him.
The princess told her:
“Take this child away, and nurse it for me, and I will give thee thy wages.” — Exodus 2:9
The mother received her child back.
And she was paid to nurse him.
The Bible does not tell us how long she continued caring for Moses before he was brought to Pharaoh's daughter.
But it tells us that when the child grew, his mother brought him to the princess, and he became her son.
Can you imagine that mother's emotions?
The relief.
The disbelief.
The trembling joy.
The knowledge that the same royal household whose decree endangered her child was now providing for his survival.
There is an almost breathtaking reversal here.
Pharaoh attempted to eliminate the Hebrew boys because he feared Israel's future.
Yet within Pharaoh's own household, a Hebrew boy was being preserved.
The palace associated with oppression became the place where the future deliverer would grow up.
And the king who tried to control history could not prevent the unfolding of God's redemptive purpose.
This does not mean every mother who loses a child will receive that child back in this life.
It does not mean every faithful act will produce an immediate miracle.
It does not mean God has promised that every painful situation will end exactly as we desire.
Scripture itself gives us many examples of righteous people who suffered terribly.
But this passage does show that human power is not ultimate.
Pharaoh could issue decrees.
He could enslave.
He could threaten.
He could command death.
But he could not cancel the covenant faithfulness of God.
Long before Moses was born, God had made promises to Abraham concerning his descendants.
In Genesis 15:13–14, God foretold that Abraham's offspring would experience oppression in a foreign land and that God would ultimately bring them out.
Exodus is not the story of God suddenly discovering Israel's suffering.
It is the story of the covenant-keeping God acting in history to deliver his people.
And the rescue of Moses belongs within that larger purpose.
There is another detail in this account that many readers overlook.
Pharaoh's daughter gave the child his name.
Exodus 2:10 says:
“And she called his name Moses: and she said, Because I drew him out of the water.”
The Hebrew form of his name is מֹשֶׁה (Mosheh).
The narrative connects the name to the Hebrew verb מָשָׁה (mashah), meaning to draw out.
Scholars also recognize that the name may reflect an Egyptian naming element associated with birth, found in Egyptian names such as Thutmose.
The biblical text, however, explicitly emphasizes the Hebrew wordplay.
Moses was drawn out of the water.
Later, through God's power, he would lead Israel through the waters of the sea.
The child who had to be rescued would become the human instrument through whom God rescued a nation.
Yet even Moses was not the final answer to humanity's deepest problem.
Because Exodus is not merely a story about escaping political oppression.
It belongs to the unfolding biblical story that ultimately leads us to Jesus Christ.
And here is where the account becomes even more profound.
Moses was a deliverer, but he was not the Savior of the world.
He was preserved from death as an infant, but he would eventually die.
He confronted Pharaoh, but he could not remove humanity's guilt before a holy God.
He led Israel out of Egypt, but he could not deliver people from the dominion of sin through his own righteousness.
The law came through Moses.
But grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.
John 1:17 declares:
“For the law was given by Moses, but grace and truth came by Jesus Christ.”
And the Gospel of Matthew records another striking connection.
When Jesus was a child, Herod sought to destroy him.
Joseph was warned in a dream and took Mary and Jesus to Egypt.
Matthew 2:15 connects Jesus' return from Egypt with Hosea 11:1:
“Out of Egypt have I called my son.”
In Hosea's original context, the words recall God's calling Israel out of Egypt.
Matthew applies that language to Jesus, presenting him as the Son who fulfills Israel's story.
The parallels between Moses and Jesus are significant, but we must understand them carefully.
Moses was preserved to serve as God's appointed leader in Israel's deliverance from slavery.
Jesus came to accomplish a greater redemption through his sinless life, sacrificial death, and resurrection.
Moses was drawn out of the water.
Jesus would enter the waters of baptism and identify himself with the people he came to save, though he himself was without sin.
Moses led Israel toward the promised land.
Jesus opens the way to reconciliation with the Father and the hope of eternal life.
Moses mediated the old covenant.
Jesus is the mediator of the new covenant.
And Hebrews 3:3 declares that Jesus is worthy of greater glory than Moses.
The ultimate hero of Scripture is not Moses.
It is Christ.
And this is why the story of Pharaoh's daughter should lead us beyond admiration for human compassion into worship of the God whose redemptive plan culminates in his Son.
Because there is a deeper question beneath the question about the princess.
What does God do with people who come from broken households, corrupt systems, shameful histories, and places nobody expects anything good to emerge from?
The Gospel answers with breathtaking hope.
Jesus Christ is not limited by the darkness of the place where your story began.
Maybe you grew up in a family where anger was normal and tenderness was rare.
Maybe the people who should have protected you became the people who wounded you.
Maybe you learned to survive by becoming hard.
Maybe you have spent years carrying the consequences of decisions you never made.
Or maybe the scandal is not what someone did to you.
Maybe it is what you did.
The lies.
The betrayal.
The cruelty.
The compromise.
The sin you keep trying to explain away.
The person you hurt.
The private life that contradicts the public image everyone admires.
And somewhere deep inside, you wonder whether someone with your history can ever become part of something holy.
Listen carefully.
Pharaoh's daughter did not become righteous merely because she performed one compassionate act.
And we do not become righteous before God simply by accumulating good deeds.
The Bible teaches that all have sinned and fall short of God's glory (Romans 3:23).
Our deepest need is not merely to become kinder versions of ourselves.
Our deepest need is reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
That reconciliation is offered by grace, received through faith, and made possible through Christ's finished work.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
And the very next verse teaches that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace does not make compassion unnecessary.
Grace gives compassion its proper place.
We do not show mercy to purchase salvation.
We show mercy because the God who saves sinners is merciful.
We do not obey Christ to make him love us.
We obey because his love has reached us and his Spirit is transforming us.
And when grace truly takes hold of a life, it begins confronting the very things that once seemed normal.
The hatred we justified.
The bitterness we protected.
The pride we disguised.
The unforgiveness we rehearsed.
The selfishness we called wisdom.
The silence we maintained because doing what was right might cost us something.
Pharaoh's daughter faced a moment in which compassion required action.
And that should make every one of us ask a difficult question.
Where am I allowing fear, comfort, loyalty, or convenience to silence the mercy God calls me to show?
Maybe you have been defending something you know is wrong simply because your family has always done it.
Maybe you have been excusing injustice because speaking against it could damage your reputation.
Maybe you have been treating a struggling person as an interruption rather than a neighbor.
Maybe you have become so consumed with protecting your own life that you have stopped noticing the people quietly drowning around you.
And perhaps the most painful possibility is this:
You have been asking God to use you in a great way while ignoring the ordinary opportunities to love someone standing right in front of you.
Not every act of obedience will become famous.
Not every compassionate decision will be recorded in history.
But faithfulness is not measured by applause.
Jesus taught that even giving a cup of cold water to one of his little ones because that person belongs to him would not go unrewarded (Matthew 10:42).
And in Luke 10, through the parable of the Good Samaritan, he confronted the tendency to separate religious knowledge from practical mercy.
The Samaritan did not merely feel sorry for the wounded man.
He acted.
He approached.
He cared.
He gave.
And Jesus said:
“Go, and do thou likewise.” — Luke 10:37
There is a kind of religion that can discuss compassion for hours while stepping around wounded people.
It can quote Scripture while refusing to forgive.
It can defend truth while delighting in cruelty.
It can sing about grace while showing none.
But Christ calls his followers to something deeper.
Truth without compromise.
Mercy without favoritism.
Holiness without hypocrisy.
Love that does not merely speak but acts.
And none of this is possible in its fullest Christian sense apart from abiding in Christ.
Jesus said in John 15:5:
“For without me ye can do nothing.”
That is why this story must not end with a princess being praised for saving a baby.
It must end with us looking to the Savior who gives new life to sinners.
Because the greatest rescue in Scripture is not a child being lifted from a basket.
It is the Son of God willingly entering our fallen world to redeem people who could never rescue themselves.
At Calvary, Jesus bore our sins.
He was crucified.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, he rose again, just as the Scriptures declare.
The cross exposes the seriousness of our sin.
The resurrection announces the victory of our Savior.
And the Gospel calls us to repent and believe in him.
Not merely to admire his compassion.
Not merely to appreciate his teachings.
But to surrender our lives to him as Lord.
Perhaps that is where this article has been leading you all along.
Not simply to the banks of the Nile.
Not merely to the royal palace.
But to the hidden places of your own heart.
The places where you have been afraid to obey God.
The places where you have mistaken religious appearance for genuine surrender.
The places where you have allowed the wounds of your past to become excuses for the choices of your present.
The places where you need forgiveness more than you need another explanation.
And here is the beautiful truth.
You do not have to pretend before Jesus.
He already knows.
He knows what happened to you.
He knows what you have done.
He knows the tears you never explained.
He knows the prayers you stopped praying.
He knows the bitterness you have been feeding.
He knows the sin you have been hiding.
And still, the Gospel calls you to come to him.
Not because your sin is insignificant.
But because his mercy is greater than the guilt of everyone who genuinely turns to him in repentance and faith.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
You may not be able to rewrite yesterday.
But in Christ, yesterday does not have to remain the master of tomorrow.
You may not be able to erase the consequences of every decision.
But through Jesus, forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and genuine transformation are possible.
That is what we mean when we say:
Not that Jesus pretends evil never happened.
Not that repentance is optional.
Not that every earthly consequence disappears.
But that the risen Christ can redeem sinners, transform hearts, and give a new identity to those who belong to him.
Second Corinthians 5:17 says:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
That promise is not reserved for people with impressive backgrounds.
It is for those who are in Christ.
The broken.
The ashamed.
The guilty.
The exhausted.
The person who has spent years trying to hide behind a smile.
The person who knows religious language but has drifted far from God.
The person who wonders whether grace could possibly reach this far.
If that is you, do not turn this into another emotional moment that fades when you close your phone.
Respond to Christ.
Confess your sin.
Turn away from what is destroying your fellowship with God.
Believe the Gospel.
Ask the Lord to make your heart tender where it has become hard.
And if you have never placed your faith in Jesus Christ, do not confuse being moved by a story with being reconciled to God.
Come to the Savior himself.
You can pray sincerely in your own words, acknowledging your sin, asking for mercy, and entrusting yourself to the crucified and risen Jesus.
A prayer is not a magic formula.
Christ is the Savior.
And he calls you to follow him.
Maybe today, your first act of obedience will be asking someone for forgiveness.
Maybe it will be refusing to participate in something dishonest.
Maybe it will be reaching out to a person you have deliberately ignored.
Maybe it will be seeking help for a struggle you have hidden for years.
Maybe it will be opening your Bible again after a long season of spiritual neglect.
Or maybe it will simply begin with a brokenhearted confession:
“Lord Jesus, I have been resisting you. Forgive me. Change me. Teach me to love what you love and hate what is evil. Help me follow you, even when obedience costs me something.”
And if those words describe what is happening inside your heart right now, I want to invite you to do something meaningful.
You do not have to share private details publicly.
But sometimes an honest response can become the beginning of a meaningful conversation, an opportunity for encouragement, or a reminder to another struggling believer that they are not alone.
And if this story brought someone to mind, do not ignore that thought.
Maybe it is a mother carrying anxiety about her child.
Maybe it is a father who feels powerless.
Maybe it is a friend trapped in shame.
Maybe it is someone who has walked away from church because the people who claimed to represent Jesus wounded them.
Maybe it is a believer who has grown comfortable with compromise.
Or someone who does not yet believe in Christ but needs to hear what the Gospel actually says about sin, mercy, and redemption.
Not merely to increase its reach, but because a message about Christ may reach someone you would never know needed it.
Send it privately to someone who might need a gentler, more personal invitation.
But I also want to speak to those who have been quietly walking with Gospel Warrior, reading these messages, sharing Scripture, and finding encouragement in this growing ministry.
There is a difference between encountering a message once and allowing biblical truth to shape your life day after day.
Spiritual growth requires more than an occasional emotional moment.
It calls for Scripture.
Prayer.
Repentance.
Fellowship.
Sound teaching.
Perseverance.
A willingness to be corrected and transformed by the Word of God.
That is why Gospel Warrior seeks to be more than a place where people read inspirational articles.
Our desire is to keep pointing people back to Jesus Christ, helping believers grow deeper in Scripture and encouraging those who are struggling to remain faithful to the Lord.
These resources are offered freely because we believe biblical encouragement and discipleship should remain accessible to people who may not have the means to purchase Christian materials.

And if this ministry has strengthened your faith, encouraged you to return to Scripture, or helped you understand the Gospel more clearly, I want to invite you to consider helping us continue and expand that work.
For those who desire to give beyond their local church commitments, it can be an additional expression of generosity and ministry partnership.
Scripture encourages believers to support faithful Gospel ministry.
Galatians 6:6 speaks of sharing good things with those who teach the Word.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That distinction matters deeply.
And while some supporters may personally regard their contribution as part of their Christian giving, it should not be presented as a mandatory biblical tithe.
Your gift does not purchase grace.
And your financial circumstances do not determine your worth before God.
But when you willingly support Gospel-centered work, you help provide practical means for that work to continue.
Some people are able to give.
Others serve by praying.
Others share Scripture with family and friends.
Others encourage someone who is struggling.
And all these acts can be meaningful expressions of Christian love when done faithfully unto the Lord.
These products can serve as reminders of biblical truth, opportunities for encouragement, and thoughtful gifts for people you love.
But the deepest reason to partner with this ministry is not merchandise.
It is the desire to see people encounter the Gospel, understand Scripture, grow in discipleship, and keep their eyes fixed on Jesus.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, those who feel spiritually distant, and even those who are still searching for answers to follow along.
Not because following a page makes someone a disciple.
But because faithful exposure to God's Word can open doors for questions, conversations, repentance, encouragement, and growth.
And because the message we proclaim is far greater than the ministry sharing it.
It is the message of Jesus Christ.
The one who came to seek and save the lost.
The one who receives repentant sinners.
The one who died for our sins and rose again.
The one who calls us out of darkness into his marvelous light.
Before you leave, return with me one final time to that river.
Picture the basket resting among the reeds.
Picture the little boy crying.
Picture his sister watching.
Picture a mother who has done everything she can and does not yet know what will happen next.
And picture the daughter of Pharaoh looking down at a child whose life has been condemned by the authority of her own father.
In that moment, the princess could not see the burning bush.
She could not see the confrontation with Pharaoh.
She could not see the night of the Passover.
She could not see the Israelites walking out of Egypt.
She could not see the sea opening before them.
And she certainly could not see the full unfolding of God's redemptive plan that would ultimately find its fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
She saw a child.
She heard him cry.
And she had compassion.
That is what the text tells us.
We do not know what became of her spiritually.
We do not know whether she ever came to worship the God of Israel.
We do not know whether she lived long enough to witness the confrontation between Moses and Pharaoh.
Scripture leaves those questions unanswered.
But it preserves her act of mercy within the story of God's deliverance.
And perhaps that is enough to confront our hearts.
Because while we are often fascinated by the great things God might accomplish tomorrow, we can overlook the simple obedience he requires of us today.
A person needs kindness.
Someone needs truth spoken in love.
A wounded heart needs compassion.
A vulnerable neighbor needs protection.
A sinner needs to hear the Gospel.
A believer needs encouragement to remain faithful.
And somewhere in the middle of an ordinary day, you may face a choice between what is comfortable and what is right.
Do not assume that a faithful act is insignificant simply because it seems small.
Do not assume that your background must determine your future.
Do not assume that the failures of those who came before you require you to repeat their sins.
And above all, do not mistake the instrument of God's providence for the God who deserves the glory.
Pharaoh's daughter showed compassion.
Moses became a deliverer.
But the Lord was faithful to his covenant.
And through the unfolding history of redemption, he has revealed the fullness of his saving grace in Jesus Christ.
So here is my final question.
When you stand before the suffering of another person, what will govern your response?
Fear?
Convenience?
The expectations of others?
Or the mercy and truth of the God you claim to follow?
What is one area of your life where you need the courage to obey God rather than surrender to fear?
Your answer may encourage someone else to take a faithful step they have been postponing.
And if you remember nothing else from this story, remember this:

Pharaoh saw a generation of children as a threat to his throne. His daughter saw one crying child as a life worth saving. But God was already preparing a deliverance greater than either of them could imagine.
May we never become so loyal to the voices of this world that we lose the courage to obey the voice of Christ.
May we never become so familiar with suffering that we stop responding with compassion.
And may we never forget that the God who preserved Moses has now made known his greatest salvation through Jesus Christ, who died and rose again so that sinners might be forgiven and made new.
The baby Pharaoh wanted erased from history became the man God used to confront him—and the Savior to whom Moses' story ultimately points is still calling broken people out of darkness into grace.
